_README: THE SIGNATURE BANK — S78 §8.5, signed by Rab 2026-08-14, built S79.
Rab's words: 'any time a zone pops up, there needs to be given a reason of what's the
issue, the highlight of it and a comment that contains the solution... banked... to reduce
latency between decision making and editing.' And why: 'new operators in the future would
not be able to discern critically without investigating the tool itself... the program
should already provide that.'
A zone arrives from the convert-time audit carrying MEASUREMENTS (line, chars, zlib,
max_trigram, excerpt) and no meaning. This file is the meaning: each entry pairs a
mechanical detector against the zone's own body window with the three things an operator
needs before touching anything — reason, highlight, solution.
EVERY MATCH IS `Inferred`, NEVER `Observed`. A detector is a proxy for a defect class, and
a proxy that is never re-checked is how S78 destroyed 418 bullet marks in Valentine by
generalising from two sampled cells (docs/32). So a match ships with `matched_on` — the
evidence that fired it — and the bench prints the tag beside the diagnosis. The operator
confirms or overrides; the machine never asserts it saw what it only pattern-matched.
An unmatched zone is `unclassified`, and that is an honest answer. Do not add a catch-all.
HOW TO WRITE AN ENTRY — the rule this bank exists to satisfy:
Explain the DEFECT, never the HISTORY. Write for an operator who has never opened a
session file and never will. A session number is provenance and belongs in `cite`; it is
not an explanation, and a reader who has to go and look it up has already lost the time
this bank was built to save. Same for internal shorthand: 'matrix mis-read', 'the S76
Beer', 'zone', 'tripwire' — say what is on the page and what to do about it.
The test: could someone who has never met this book read the entry and know what they
are looking at, and what would be destroyed if they got it wrong? The first version of F
failed that test in front of Rab, which is how the rule got written.
Seeded from Valentine's A-F bank (S78 §16), which is the scoring rubric for any rival
engine (S78 §18.3: measure on the real corpus, score named defects, never vibes).

signatures.name: decoder token-loop
signatures.reason: The OCR decoder got stuck and emitted the same token sequence hundreds of times. This is not a layout problem — it is generated text that was never on the page, and it has usually eaten whatever real content followed it.
signatures.highlight: The repeated phrase at the zone line. Compare its length against the surrounding paragraphs: the loop is the block that compresses far better than prose ever does.
signatures.solution: Collapse it (⌫). A collapse removes noise and restores nothing — say so and do not claim credit for content. Then read the source page: whatever the loop displaced is still missing and needs a crop or a transcription — on one book a loop like this had swallowed an entire numbered item, and collapsing it made the gap visible rather than fixing it.

signatures.name: embed severing a table header
signatures.reason: A repair image was inserted between a table's header row and its |---| delimiter. Markdown then stops recognising the table entirely, so the whole grid renders as raw pipes — the repair broke more than it fixed.
signatures.highlight: The ![[...]] line sitting immediately below a | header | row and above (or instead of) its delimiter.
signatures.solution: Move the embed to AFTER the table's last row. Bench.repair() inserts after the zone line with no structural check, so this is a bench defect, not an operator error — the same insertion is correct three lines lower.
signatures.auto: yes — move the embed below the table

signatures.name: column-wrap as literal
signatures.reason:
The converter preserved a visual line-wrap inside a table cell as a literal
. The content is all present and correct; only its shape is wrong.
signatures.highlight:
Cells containing
where the text either side is one continuous phrase.
signatures.solution:
Join the fragments with a space and delete the
. Nothing is missing here, so this must NOT be treated as an omission — do not crop a page for it.

signatures.name: row-merge
signatures.reason:
Several table rows were collapsed into a single row, with
standing in for the row breaks. The cells are present but their alignment to columns is lost, so the table asserts relationships that were never on the page.
signatures.highlight:
One table row far longer than its neighbours, carrying repeated
at consistent intervals.
signatures.solution:
Split on
back into separate rows, then check each against the source page — the column alignment is exactly what cannot be recovered from the markdown alone, and a wrong alignment is worse than a missing one.
signatures.auto: partial — the split is mechanical, the alignment is not

signatures.name: rotated label shredded
signatures.reason:
A label printed vertically on the page (a rotated axis or column header) was read one character per row. `_ S A R
T
E
G Ϋ́` is STRATEGY. The letters survive; the word does not.
signatures.highlight: Three or more consecutive lines whose entire content is one or two characters.
signatures.solution: Read the letters in order, reconstruct the word, and write it back as a single cell. Confirm against the source page before writing — the reading order of a rotated label is not always top-to-bottom.
signatures.auto: structure yes, the word needs an eye

signatures.name: matrix mis-read
signatures.reason: This is a grid, not a table with empty columns. The rows are items — questions, tasks, criteria. The columns are sources. A • where a row meets a column means 'this source covers this item', so the • marks ARE the content. The column headings were printed sideways on the page, and the converter cannot read rotated text, so the top of every column came out blank. That is why a dozen columns can look empty while carrying hundreds of marks.
signatures.highlight: Count the • marks in this zone before touching anything. Then look at the source page: the headings you are missing run vertically across the top of the grid, usually reading bottom-to-top.
signatures.solution: Do NOT delete the blank-looking columns — the • marks in them are the answer to 'which source do I use for this'. Read the sideways headings off the page and type them into the header row, leaving every • exactly where it is. If the headings are unreadable, crop the page in as an image and leave the table alone: a lost layout can be rebuilt, lost marks cannot. Before you edit any row here, print the whole row and look at it — sampling two cells is how a previous session concluded thirteen populated columns were empty and removed 418 marks.
signatures.auto: unknown — the one signature that has already caused data loss
